newsitem.title: INDIA: Separatists launch strike on eve of Kashmir poll.
newsitem.headline: Separatists launch strike on eve of Kashmir poll.

text.p: Separatist groups called a general strike and masked canvassers attempted to rally support for their candidates on Sunday as the Himalayan state of Jammu and Kashmir prepared for Monday's state assembly polls.
Indian security forces were concentrated in the 34 assembly constituencies that go to the polls for the second leg of voting in the first state assembly elections to be held in nine years.

The separatist 30-party Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference was awaiting the response to a call for a two-day general strike while Moslem militants continued to enforce their closure of government offices, schools and banks which started on August 24.
Separatists opposing the polls have accused the government of intimidating people to vote.

"An election in which political supporters wear masks and people are coerced to cast their vote with all kinds of threats is a laughable way to solve Kashmir's problems," Hurriyat spokesman Abdul Ghani told Reuters.

The four-stage election to the 87-seat assembly has been marred by violent clashes in which more than 20 political workers have died. The first stage of the polls, involving 26 constituencies in mainly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state, was held on September 7.
Politicians said the presence of Indian security forces in the voting constituencies had not deterred rival groups and separatists from attacking opponents.
"The fact that political supporters are forced to wear masks does suggest an element of fear," a defence spokesman told Reuters. "But their percentage is low. It isn't so alarming."
Dozens of militant groups seeking a separate nation or a merger with neighbouring Pakistan are fighting Indian rule. Islamabad has denied Indian charges that it is arming the militants.
India, which controls two-thirds of the region, does not recognise Pakistan-held Azad, or "Free", Kashmir and keeps 23 seats vacant in the Jammu and Kashmir state assembly.
India called the polls after a national debate in which most major political parties agreed it was the only way to restore democracy in the strife-torn region.
More than 20,000 people have been killed since an armed revolt began in 1990, forcing out the then state chief minister Farooq Abdullah and leading to the imposition of direct rule by New Delhi.

Abdullah's National Conference party boycotted parliamentary elections in May but agreed to contest the local elections after New Delhi agreed to open talks on extensive autonomy for Kashmir with the new state government.
Abdullah, who survived an assassination attempt last week, had objected to the presence of government-backed armed militia groups in Kashmir, saying they were a hindrance to the polls.
But sources in the security forces say his party has won over some of the militia leaders as had the Congress party of former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.

Government-backed militia leader Kuka Parey's Awami League party has put up its own candidate in areas where it is influential. The Janata Dal party of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda is also a major challenger in the fray.
Voting in the remaining constituencies is scheduled for September 21 and 30.
